passage: “Aadhya, just say it,” said Ira, sitting on the sleepover sofa with the blanket around her. The others were still up watching a film. Aadhya's eyes were wet. “I miss Mummy.” “Me too, sometimes,” said Ira. “Do you want to call her?” Aadhya nodded. Ira asked her mother if they could use her phone. The call was short. Aadhya's mother said, “I'll see you at nine in the morning. Sleep well.” Aadhya held her teddy tight. She said, “I feel better.” Ira said, “It's okay to miss somebody.” They lay down next to each other and watched the end of the film.

qa.q: What did Aadhya hold tight?
qa.a: Her teddy.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling at the sleepover?
qa.a: She was homesick and missed her mother, and the wet eyes showed it.

qa.q: What helped Aadhya feel better?
qa.a: Talking about it, calling her mother and holding the teddy, and Ira telling her it is okay to miss somebody.

qa.q: How might Ira have understood Aadhya's feelings?
qa.a: Ira said she sometimes misses someone too, so she likely saw it as an ordinary feeling.

grounding: A child at a sleepover feels homesick, and talking, a comfort item and a call help.

passage: I still remember my first school camp, in a forest outside Pune. I was ten. The bunk beds smelled of dust, and after lights out I heard a girl whisper into her pillow. I felt a lump in my throat too. I missed my grandmother's hands and her bedtime stories. Noor, my bunkmate, said, “I miss my dog.” We whispered about home till the lump got smaller. In the morning our teacher told us we could call home at five. I marked five on my palm with a pen. It was strange, but missing them felt like proof that I loved them. Hafsa.

qa.q: How old was the writer at the first school camp?
qa.a: Ten.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling after lights out?
qa.a: Hafsa felt homesick, missing the grandmother's hands and bedtime stories, and the lump in the throat shows it.

qa.q: What helped Hafsa and Noor cope with missing home?
qa.a: Whispering about home, and the planned call at five that the teacher promised.

qa.q: How might Noor have felt hearing Hafsa's admission?
qa.a: Noor probably felt less alone, since Noor shared missing the dog and the two of them talked until the lump got smaller.

grounding: A child at a camp feels homesick and longing for family, and talking and a planned call help, showing healthy attachment.

passage: Camp leader's note, night two. Vinita, Group C. Rashmi was quiet at dinner and left most of her khichdi. At campfire she sat at the edge, hugging the knitted elephant her Nani made. When I sat beside her, she whispered, “I miss Mummy. I want to go home.” I told her missing home means she has people she loves, and that lots of campers feel it on the second night. We made a plan: she keeps the elephant by her pillow, and tomorrow at seven she calls home from my phone. I checked on her at lights-out. She was asleep, the elephant under her chin.

qa.q: Who made Rashmi's knitted elephant?
qa.a: Her Nani made the knitted elephant.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling as she hugged the elephant at the campfire?
qa.a: Rashmi felt homesick and sad, missing her mother and wanting to go home.

qa.q: What steps did Vinita take to help Rashmi?
qa.a: She listened, said missing home shows love, kept the elephant by her pillow, planned a call home at seven and checked on her at lights-out.

qa.q: Why might Vinita say missing home means having people you love?
qa.a: Vinita wanted Rashmi to see homesickness as a sign of healthy attachment, not something to be ashamed of.

grounding: Shows a child's homesickness at camp and how talking, a comfort item and a planned call help.

passage: Tuesday night. Ankita's diary. My third night at Nani's in the village. The days are fun: the calves, the mango tree, the pond. But at night I miss Papa so much my chest hurts. I brought his old blue T-shirt to sleep in, and it still smells a bit like him. Nani saw me crying and didn't say, “Don't be silly.” She said, “Missing someone means you love them. Shall we call him?” She dialled and called out, “Harish, your daughter wants you!” Papa told me the cat knocked over his tea. I laughed. We decided to call every night at eight. Only four more nights. The T-shirt helps.

qa.q: What did Ankita bring to sleep in?
qa.a: Ankita brought Papa's old blue T-shirt.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling at night at Nani's?
qa.a: Ankita felt homesick, missing Papa so much her chest hurt.

qa.q: What helped Ankita cope with missing Papa?
qa.a: Talking with Nani, the comfort of Papa's T-shirt and a planned call every night at eight.

qa.q: How did Nani respond to Ankita's tears?
qa.a: Nani didn't dismiss them; she said missing someone means you love them and offered to call Papa.

grounding: Shows a child's longing for a parent while away, and a comfort item, talking and planned calls helping.

passage: On the second evening of the school's village-stay camp, Shreya sat by the well while the others played kabaddi. She kept looking at the road. Her little brother Bhupen had cried when the bus left, and now she couldn't stop thinking about him: whether he'd found his torch, who was reading him his story. The teacher came and sat on the edge of the well. “Missing someone?” Shreya nodded. “My brother. He's scared of the dark.” “That's a big-sister feeling,” the teacher said. “Want to call him before his bedtime?” At eight, Shreya told Bhupen a story over the phone, from memory. Afterwards she went and joined the kabaddi game.

qa.q: What is Bhupen scared of?
qa.a: Bhupen is scared of the dark.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling as she kept looking at the road?
qa.a: Shreya felt homesick and worried about her little brother, missing him and wondering who was reading his story.

qa.q: How did the teacher help Shreya?
qa.a: The teacher noticed, named the feeling kindly and offered a call before his bedtime, so she could tell him a story.

qa.q: How did Bhupen react when the bus left?
qa.a: Bhupen cried when the bus left, showing he missed his sister too.

grounding: Shows a child missing family at camp, and talking and a planned call helping her join in again.

passage:
On the second night at the lakeside camp in Scotland, Yara lay in her bunk with her face pressed into Mum's old blue scarf, the one that still smelled of their kitchen. Her throat ached. She could picture Dad burning the pancakes on Saturday, her little brother's socks everywhere.

Freya, the camp leader, found her by torchlight. "Missing home?" Yara nodded into the scarf. Freya sat on the floor by the bunk. "That ache means you've got people worth missing. Tell me one thing you'd be doing right now."
"Fighting with my brother over the TV."
They both laughed a little. "Your call home is booked for six tomorrow. Keep the scarf close till then."

Yara breathed in the kitchen smell and, eventually, slept.

qa.q: What did Yara press her face into?
qa.a: Mum's old blue scarf.

qa.q: What was Yara feeling on the second night?
qa.a: Homesick and longing for her family, with an aching throat as she pictured home.

qa.q: What three things did Freya use to help?
qa.a: She got Yara talking about home, encouraged her to keep the comfort scarf close, and reminded her of the call booked for six tomorrow.

qa.q: How did Freya see Yara's homesickness?
qa.a: As a healthy sign that Yara has people worth missing, not something to be ashamed of.

grounding: It shows a child homesick at camp, eased by talking, a comfort item and a planned call, with missing family framed as healthy attachment.
